facts.claim: Sinek builds the book on James Carse's distinction: a finite game has known players, fixed rules and an agreed end with a winner (soccer); an infinite game has known and unknown players, rules that can change, and the aim of keeping the game going.
Sinek applies it to business, relationships and education: there is no final winner, so a finite mindset (play to beat others) is the wrong one for an infinite game.
Finite-minded leaders chase near-term profit and react to disruption and to specific rivals; infinite-minded leaders aim to stay in the game and grow stronger from setbacks.
Sinek cites a study that the lifespan of S&P 500 companies fell from about 61 years to about 18.
Five practices: advance a just cause, build trusting teams, study worthy rivals, practice existential flexibility, show the courage to lead.

Sinek was invited to education summits by both Apple and Microsoft. At Microsoft's, presenters spent much of their time on how to beat Apple; at Apple's, presenters talked about how Apple was helping teachers teach.
A worthy rival is a competitor who is better than you at something and so shows you where to improve.
Sinek says he spent years treating the author Adam Grant as a competitor; after meeting him he concluded that how he had seen Grant had to do with himself, not with Grant (paraphrase).
Summaries of the book use Microsoft as the example of rival-fixation: it answered the iPod with the Zune, which did not catch on, and Steve Ballmer dismissed the iPhone as not worth replicating.
A trusting team is one whose members feel safe expressing feelings, asking for help, discussing problems and admitting mistakes.
Where trust is missing, members hide mistakes and fake expertise instead of asking for help, so problems pile up unaddressed.
Leaders set the tone by listening to concerns and letting people raise issues without fear of repercussions.
The trusting-teams chapters use Shell Oil and the US Marine Corps Officer Candidate School as examples (details not retrieved).
Sinek defines a just cause as 'a specific vision of a future state that does not yet exist'; a valid one is for something, inclusive, service-oriented, resilient and idealistic.
Sinek says the five practices should be adopted together.
A reviewer notes that Carse acknowledges everyone plays finite games, and that Sinek puts a negative connotation on anything finite.

Sinek claims that adopting a healthier attitude toward rivals improves resilience, resource management, innovation and personal integrity; the worthy-rival chapter opens with an autobiographical story, which one reviewer finds overly romanticized.

Sinek (December 2019 Army Profession Forum talk and interview, tied to the book's 'Building Trusting Teams' practice) calls psychological safety the foundation for trusting teams, a 'biological and anthropological concept' not up for debate; people must feel safe enough to perform at their best.

In that talk his examples of what people must be free to say: 'I made a mistake' and 'I need help'; if soldiers cannot say them, he says the leader has failed. High performers with low trust may deliver short-term results but damage the organization over time.

Summary of the practice: assess members on performance and earned trust. High performance with low trust is the person to watch (hoards information, takes credit, puts own career first); low performance with high trust may be worth keeping if coachable.
When people feel safe they speak up, admit mistakes, ask for help and raise concerns, which improves information flow.

In the same talk Sinek called trust 'the root of all friendships, relationships, trusting teams' and said it lets people rely on each other 'with our frailty, with our insecurity'; he also said admitting fear or doubt about one's qualifications should be possible.
